title: Berkshire Operating Earnings Fall 5.8% as Buybacks Hit $9.6 Billion
excerpt: Third-quarter operating earnings slipped to $12.705 billion on weaker insurance results, while Berkshire more than doubled buybacks to $9.6 billion and its shares rose more than 5% in a week when the S&P 500 fell almost 2.7%.
body:
• Berkshire Hathaway's third-quarter operating earnings fell 5.8% to $12.705 billion from $13.485 billion a year earlier, weighed down by a 43% drop in insurance underwriting profit.
  • The company bought back about $9.6 billion of its own stock in the quarter, more than double the $4.5 billion in the second quarter and, according to Barron's, probably its highest quarterly figure ever.
  • Berkshire shares rose more than 5% this week while the S&P 500 fell almost 2.7% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 3.4%, as investors moved out of slumping technology stocks amid fears that AI data-centre spending will not pay off, according to CNBC reporting.
  • For holders, the reader-relevant split is simple: operating earnings per Class A share were $8,907, against an average FactSet forecast of $8,821.84 from four analysts surveyed — reported results, not expectations, are the $12.705 billion figure above.

Berkshire Hathaway reported third-quarter operating earnings of $12.705 billion on Saturday, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion a year earlier, as weaker insurance results offset growth at its railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses. The company disclosed the results in its earnings release and quarterly filing, according to Barron's coverage of the release.

Net earnings, which include gains and losses on Berkshire's stock portfolio, fell to $22.112 billion, or $15,502 per Class A share, from $30.796 billion a year earlier. Berkshire itself tells investors to look past those quarterly investment swings, arguing that they do not show how its businesses performed. Investment gains were smaller than a year earlier, which explains much of the sharper fall in net earnings compared with operating earnings.

Reported versus expected

Operating earnings came to $8,907 per Class A share, the Associated Press reported, against an average forecast of $8,821.84 from four analysts surveyed by FactSet. Barron's put its own estimate at $8,910 per Class A share and described the overall earnings figure as in line with the consensus estimate. The buyback figure, by contrast, was above expectations, Barron's said.

Insurance weighed on the quarter

After-tax insurance underwriting profit fell to $1.352 billion from $2.369 billion, a drop of about 43%. Geico, the auto insurer, saw pretax underwriting earnings shrink to $982 million from $1.773 billion. Geico's loss ratio rose 5.1 percentage points to 76.6%, which Berkshire attributed to claims that were both more frequent and more expensive, along with lower average premiums per policy. Insurance investment income fell 14.1% to $2.734 billion after tax, which Berkshire said reflected lower short-term interest rates.

The other large businesses grew. BNSF railroad after-tax earnings rose 19.3% to $1.729 billion on higher freight volumes and better efficiency. Berkshire Hathaway Energy gained 8.3% to $1.612 billion, and manufacturing, service and retailing rose 11.8% to $4.042 billion.

The third-quarter operating result was also affected by currency swings on Berkshire's yen-related borrowings: Barron's noted a currency loss of $343 million, compared with a $331 million gain a year earlier, and calculated that excluding the swing, operating earnings were down less than 1% year over year to about $13 billion.

A record pace of buybacks, and the cash pile

Berkshire bought back about $9.6 billion of its own stock in the third quarter, more than double the $4.5 billion in the second quarter, lifting repurchases for the first nine months of 2026 to about $14.4 billion. It was Greg Abel's third quarter as chief executive; he took over from Warren Buffett in January, according to the Associated Press. Barron's said the figure indicates Abel and controlling shareholder Warren Buffett felt the stock was inexpensive in the period, and estimated Berkshire continued buying back about $2 billion of shares in October, with the pace slowing as the stock price rose above $800,000 a share for Class A shares.

On cash, the measures need to be kept separate. Cash and equivalents including Treasury bills, excluding cash held at the railroad and utility businesses, totalled $352 billion at the end of September, compared with $360 billion on June 30, according to Barron's. A broader measure that adds railroad and utility cash and Treasury purchases that had not yet settled rose to $377.4 billion from $365.5 billion on June 30. Barron's said the lower $352 billion figure reflected the acquisition of home builder Taylor Morrison for almost $7 billion in cash in July and the heavy buyback activity.

Why the shares surged this week

The earnings arrived after a strong week for the stock. Berkshire's Class B shares rose more than 5% this week while the S&P 500 fell almost 2.7% and the Nasdaq Composite fell 3.4% and entered correction territory, more than 10% below its most recent high, before recovering some ground on Friday, according to CNBC reporting carried by Zot News. One month ago, Berkshire's B shares were underperforming the S&P 500 by 13.6 percentage points for the year; after three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire now leads the benchmark by 5.8 percentage points.

Berkshire is not entirely removed from the AI sell-off. As of June 30 it held about 106 million shares of Alphabet, with a market value of $37.8 billion, then its third-largest equity holding. Since then Alphabet's share classes have dropped around 20%, reducing the stake to about $30.2 billion. Bloomberg suggested, in reporting quoted by CNBC, that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."

What to watch next

Berkshire's third-quarter portfolio disclosure for the period ending September 30 is due to show whether it adjusted its Alphabet position. The Class A shares ended Friday at $856,612 and the Class B shares at $570.89, according to Barron's, with both classes up about 13.5% so far this year. Whether buybacks continue at the third-quarter pace will depend on price: Barron's noted Berkshire is price-sensitive in its repurchases, and the October pace already appeared to slow as the share price rose.
